title: The History of the Electric Car
metadata: U.S. Department of Energy; Rebecca Matulka | 2014-09-15 | Historical overview as published in 2014
scopeAndLocation: Scope and location: Primarily United States, with international origins acknowledged; The birth of the electric vehicle; The early rise and fall of the electric car; Gas shortages spark interest in electric vehicles; Environmental concern drives electric vehicles forward
supports: Supports: Electric vehicle development arose from multiple nineteenth-century battery and motor advances, without a single unambiguous inventor; Electric cars attracted urban users; US gasoline-car adoption benefited from cost, electric starters, roads and fuel availability; 1970s oil supply concerns revived US electric-vehicle research interest; 1976 legislation authorised federal R&D and demonstration support; US environmental and energy regulations renewed interest during the 1990s
limits: Limits: Institutional retrospective, not a contemporaneous primary document for nineteenth-century events; US-centred account must not be presented as a complete global chronology; No early global market share, unqualified first invention or current market forecast taken from the page; Its 2014 forecasts and contemporary totals are excluded

title: Batteries Not Included
metadata: Science Museum; Kathleen McIlvenna | 2010-10-05 | Historical battery development
scopeAndLocation: Scope and location: Battery technology history; Opening discussion of rechargeable batteries, paragraph naming Gaston Planté
supports: Supports: Gaston Planté developed the lead-acid rechargeable battery in 1859
limits: Limits: Museum historical account, not original 1859 experimental documentation; Used only for the lead-acid milestone; The page's separate lithium-battery introduction date is not used; the Nobel source is used for lithium-ion commercialisation chronology; No claim of a complete, linear replacement of lead-acid by lithium-ion

title: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2019: Popular information
metadata: Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences / Nobel Prize Outreach; Ann Fernholm | 2019-10, prize educational material; exact page publication day not displayed in retrieved body | Lithium-ion battery research and commercialisation history
scopeAndLocation: Scope and location: International scientific development; Opening overview; High voltages when lithium ions hide in cobalt oxide; Yoshino builds the first commercially viable lithium-ion battery; The lithium-ion battery – necessary for a fossil fuel-free society
supports: Supports: Whittingham's rechargeable-lithium work in the 1970s, Goodenough's high-voltage oxide cathode work in 1980, Yoshino's carbon-anode configuration in 1985; Commercial lithium-ion battery sales began in 1991 according to the prize account; The 2019 chemistry prize recognised Goodenough, Whittingham and Yoshino for lithium-ion battery development
limits: Limits: Authoritative prize-body synthesis of scientific history; not the original papers or patents; Avoids treating the prize as a complete list of contributors; Does not establish an immediate automotive market breakthrough in 1991 or the safety of all lithium-ion systems

title: Global EV Outlook 2026: Trends in electric cars; Executive summary
metadata: International Energy Agency | 2026-05-20, verified on report landing page | 2025 historical estimate; 2026 projections excluded from this history
scopeAndLocation: Scope and location: Global; China; Europe; United States; Electric car sales topped 20 million globally in 2025; Across the three major electric car markets; notes defining electric cars; executive-summary opening
supports: Supports: 2025 electric-car sales exceeded 20 million, grew 20%, and represented 25% of new-car sales globally; 2025 sales penetration was nearly 55% in China, 28% in Europe and just under 10% in the United States; The report defines electric cars as BEV and PHEV
limits: Limits: IEA analytical compilation, not a single direct official worldwide registration census; underlying sources include EV Volumes, ACEA, EAFO and country submissions; Sales share is a share of new-car sales, not the vehicle stock, revenues, all road vehicles or fuel-cell market; Europe is not identical to European Union; Publication date verified at https://www.iea.org/reports/global-ev-outlook-2026; 2026 forecasts are not 2026 actuals

scopeAndLocation: Scope and location: Global; China; Europe; United States; Electric cars are BEV plus PHEV including EREV; Electric car sales; Across the three major electric car markets
supports: Supports: 2025 electric car sales exceeded 20 million, rose 20% and reached 25% of new cars. BEVs were 65% of electric car sales. China exceeded 13 million and Europe reached 4.2 million; US sales were about 1.5 million.
limits: Limits: IEA estimates, partly based on commercial datasets. Europe is not EU. Rounded totals cannot support precise OEM shares; EREV must not be added again to PHEV.

metadata: IEA | 2026-05-20 | 2026 Q1; May 2026 forecast for 2026
scopeAndLocation: Scope and location: Global; BEV plus PHEV electric cars; Electric cars are poised to make up a greater share of total car sales in 2026

limits: Limits: A dated forecast, not 2026 actual sales or an October nowcast. Scenario and policy assumptions can change.

title: Global EV Outlook 2026 Electric vehicle batteries
scopeAndLocation: Scope and location: Global; EV battery deployment by capacity; nameplate battery manufacturing capacity separately; Electric vehicle battery deployment; Battery industry trends; Battery manufacturing and trade
supports: Supports: EV battery deployment reached 1.2 TWh. LFP exceeded 55% of deployed EV battery capacity. Battery nameplate capacity exceeded 4 TWh; China held over 80%. CATL, BYD, LG Energy Solution and Panasonic illustrate cell manufacturers.
limits: Limits: GWh shares are not vehicle shares. Nameplate capacity covers different applications and is not usable output; do not divide deployment by nameplate to infer plant utilisation. Pack price averages include stationary storage.

scopeAndLocation: Scope and location: Global; Public charging points, not stations or private chargers; Public charging infrastructure rollout further accelerated in 2025
supports: Supports: Public charging points exceeded 7 million at end 2025 after nearly 1.8 million additions. Rated capacity, vehicle compatibility and access to private charging matter as well as point counts.
limits: Limits: A point is not a station. Nameplate power is not delivered energy, availability or average charging speed; figures include light-duty vehicles beyond passenger cars where stated.

title: Global EV Outlook 2026 Manufacturing and trade
scopeAndLocation: Scope and location: Global; Electric car production, trade and maker headquarters distinguished; Electric car manufacturing and trade
supports: Supports: Nearly 22 million electric cars were produced in 2025; China produced nearly 75%. About one-quarter of production was traded internationally.
limits: Limits: Production location, brand ownership and sale destination are different. Exports need not equal final registrations abroad; production is not sales.
